domain: Earth Womb, Savior of Hell Beings
meaning: The Earth-Womb — bodhisattva of the great vow to empty the hells (kṣiti 'earth' + garbha 'womb')

pronunciation.approximation: kshih-tih-GUR-bhuh — the kṣ is one conjunct sound; the bh is aspirated.
pronunciation.note: Kṣitigarbha is kṣiti, "earth" (from √kṣi, "to dwell, abide" — Monier-Williams), + garbha, "womb, inner chamber, treasury": "the Earth-Womb," the earth as the storehouse that holds and hides all treasure. East Asia translated rather than transliterated: Chinese Dìzàng, "Earth-Store," Japanese Jizō. The restoration's whole distinctiveness is carried by one letter — the retroflex ṣ inside the kṣ conjunct — which the ASCII "Ksitigarbha" writes but cannot show. Tier-1 by rule.

kin.label: Tibetan
kin.form: Sa yi snying po, "Essence of the Earth"

domains.title: The Earth-Womb
domains.subtitle: The Great Vow, the Six-Ringed Staff, and the Hells Emptied One Being at a Time
domains.lead: Kṣitigarbha is the bodhisattva of the greatest vow ever sworn: not to attain Buddhahood until the hells are emptied — the monk-robed guardian of the dead, the traveler, and the child, who accepted the loneliest commission in Buddhism: to fill the age between one Buddha's passing and the next one's coming.

cards.name: The Great Vow
cards.desc: "Until the hells are empty, I shall not become a Buddha" — the pledge that defines him.

cards.name: The Khakkhara
cards.desc: The six-ringed monk's staff: its jingle warns the small creatures, and its point opens the gates of hell.

cards.name: The Wish-Fulfilling Jewel
cards.desc: The cintāmaṇi in his hand: the light he carries into the darkest of the six realms.

cards.name: The Six Jizō
cards.desc: One for each realm of rebirth: the six forms in which he patrols the whole wheel of existence.

symbols.name: The monk's robe and shaven head
symbols.meaning: The only great bodhisattva who refuses princely ornament: humility as the uniform of the vow

symbols.name: The staff of six rings
symbols.meaning: The sound of mercy approaching: the rings ring so beings may step aside, and hell's doors not stay shut

symbols.name: The red bib
symbols.meaning: The cloth mothers tie on roadside Jizō: the grief and gratitude of the living made visible

mythology.lead: Kṣitigarbha's mythology is the story of a vow repeated across lifetimes — a brahmin daughter, a king — each life renewing the same impossible promise.

myths.title: The Commission in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven
myths.text: The Sūtra of the Past Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva is set in the heaven of the Thirty-Three, where the Buddha preaches for his mother's sake before his passing. There he recounts Kṣitigarbha's long record of vows and formally entrusts to him all beings of the coming age — the interval between Śākyamuni's parinirvāṇa and Maitreya's arrival. The sūtra's most quoted line is the vow itself: until the hells are empty, he shall not become a Buddha; only when every being is saved will he accept awakening. The Sanskrit original is lost; the text survives chiefly in Chinese and Tibetan, and its promise survived everything.

myths.title: The Brahmin Daughter
myths.text: The sūtra's most beloved past life is a daughter's. A pious brahmin girl's mother died slandering the Dharma, and the daughter, selling all she had to make offerings, was granted a vision of the Avīci hell — where she learned that her merit had already lifted her mother toward heaven. Seeing the legions of the damned who had no daughter to save them, she vowed to deliver them all: the vow was born of filial piety and outgrew the family in a single act. In East Asia this story fused his cult with the Ghost Festival itself, the season of the dead.

myths.title: The Silla Prince of Jiuhua
myths.text: In the eighth century a Korean prince of Silla, Jin Qiaojue, came to Mount Jiuhua in Anhui and practiced there in austerity until his death; the mountain's monks, finding his body uncorrupted, enshrined him as Dìzàng's own emanation, and Jiuhuashan became the bodhisattva's bodhimaṇḍa — one of China's four sacred Buddhist mountains. His "flesh body" is venerated there still, and Dìzàng's birthday on the thirtieth of the seventh lunar month closes the Ghost Month across the Chinese world.

myths.title: Jizō of the Riverbank
myths.text: Japan made him the most loved figure in its folk religion: Jizō, the roadside monk. In the tale of Sai-no-kawara, the dry riverbed of the underworld where the souls of dead children pile their little towers of stones, demons come to scatter the piles — and Jizō gathers the children into his great sleeves and shelters them. Parents tie red bibs and caps on his statues; travelers claim him for the roads; the Six Jizō stand at village boundaries for the six realms. The bodhisattva of the loneliest vow became the companion of every road.

lore.syncretism: East Asia rebuilt him in its own image without touching the vow: China seated him over the Ten Kings of the underworld bureaucracy and wove him into the Ghost Festival's calendar; Korea's Jijang shares the Jiuhua inheritance; Japan fused Jizō with the roadside protector-deities of the old highways and the cult of dead children. Tibet received him as Sa yi snying po among the eight great bodhisattvas, though without the underworld portfolio. Comparatists place him among the great psychopomps — but note the difference: he does not guide the dead out; he goes in and stays until the last one leaves.
lore.culturalLegacy: Kṣitigarbha is the working religion of grief in East Asia: the mizuko kuyō services in which Japanese parents memorialize lost pregnancies are held before him; the bibbed stone Jizō is Japan's commonest roadside sight; and Dìzàng's temples anchor the Chinese underworld's moral map. His vow has become the Mahāyāna's most quoted sentence — the standard against which every other pledge of compassion is measured — and his monk's robe the proof that the highest bodhisattva need not look like a king.
lore.extendedMeditation: Kṣitigarbha's vow is logically impossible, and that is the point: compassion does not audit. He accepted the assignment with no finish line — the hells refill as fast as they empty — and the tradition honors him not for succeeding but for not leaving. Every caregiver, every night-shift worker, every parent beside a hospital cot knows the shape of his job: you stay until they are out. He simply made "they" mean everyone.

sources.name: Kṣitigarbha Sūtra (Sūtra of the Past Vows)

lore.archaeology: His surviving landscape is vast: Jiuhuashan's temple-mountain, with the flesh-body hall of the Silla prince, remains an active pilgrimage city; the Dunhuang caves preserve banner-paintings of Dìzàng enthroned among the Ten Kings of hell, the earliest great cycle of his iconography. Japan's material record is the stone Jizō itself — uncounted thousands of carved figures at village edges, crossroads, and temple yards, from medieval stelae to today's bibbed statues — the densest distribution of any Buddhist image in the archipelago.
